items.title: Monumental year takes US rising star Ashlin Barry from 'I could barely walk' to 'memory that will last a lifetime'
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
New under-23 road world champion Ashlin Barry didn't have a lot of time to celebrate a gold medal and a rainbow jersey as one of the most extraordinary rewards for a 19th birthday three weeks ago. After his solo conquest across the slopes of Mont Royal in the U23 road race at the UCI Road World Championships, he went straight to Los Angeles for a training camp on the track with Team USA and then headed to Shanghai for the UCI Track World Championships.

There's no time to rest on any laurels for Barry, as his sights are set on a version of California dreaming at the Los Angeles Olympic Games, now 639 days away.

"At the moment, I'm putting a lot of focus on the track in Team Pursuit, and then maybe qualifying for the Omnium, or something will come as a byproduct of that. If I could qualify for the road [at the Olympic Games], that would be pretty cool. But I think I have to take a step up physically from where I am now to make that selection," Barry told in an exclusive one-on-one interview in Montréal.

"In terms of preparation, there's a lot going into our team pursuit now, and whether it's like a bunch event on the track or qualifying for the road, I think those will fall into place."

Barry has a huge balancing act to manage across multiple disciplines, global travel and a new commitment through 2029 to the Visma-Lease a Bike Development squad that could see him jump to the WorldTour team sooner rather than later.

Just two years before, he impressed with a silver medal in the Omnium at the Junior Track World Championships, sweeping US national titles in the road race and time trial, and winning junior and elite national titles in the Madison.

In 2025, after graduating from high school, he came second in the junior men's E3 Saxo Classic and Paris-Roubaix, earned a silver medal in the junior time trial at World Roads and the gold medal in the US Pro junior time trial national championships.

But his plan to make a statement on the track was derailed at the start of 2026, and he kept goals with his new Visma team modest.

"This was a tough year because I was supposed to do Pan Am Championships in February. I crashed on my knee in January, so I wasn't able to ride my bike. I could barely walk," he recalled.

"Things didn't go as planned. I was in Spain at training camp. Then I had to get some stitches in my knee, and I couldn't bend it. It could have been a lot worse, but it was a couple of weeks off the bike, and then I missed the track because of that."

While his track maturation was put on hold in the spring, he jumped into the fray in the Olympia's Tour at the end of March, earning two podiums. He then finished fifth in the U23 In Flanders Fields and then won the US Pro U23 road race and came in fourth in the US Pro elite men's road race the next day.

So when he finished one step off the podium in the U23 time trial at Montreal Road Worlds, he had modest expectations yet again. When asked two days before the U23 road race what he expected, the teen simply stated that he could be competitive on Friday but was "not going in thinking I have a super-high chance of getting a medal".

A gold medal and rainbow jersey were the result of a solo ride on his biggest stage yet. Barry called the win in the men's U23 road race "a memory that will last a lifetime". It was a monumental final 30 kilometres of the 174km contest, as the teenager carried the colours of Team USA to the win, and enthralled family and friends from two countries as a dual citizen of the US and Canada.

Even as he held his pace at the front of the race for the 12th of 13 circuits across Mont Royal, he said he wasn't sure he was strong enough to maintain a 40-second advantage. However, once he crested the major climb the final time and added to his solo lead, he let himself believe he could win, encouraged by supporters around the course.

"Once I was away, I just committed. It really felt like a home race out there," he told the media, including , in Montreal. "It was just unreal being out there, seeing so many friends, seeing my family. I could hear my dog barking on the side of the course."

He now registers an entry in the family's journal of success in Montreal, his mother and former US elite women's road race national champion Dede Demet-Barry having won a pro race in Montreal in 2002, five years before Barry was born. His father and two-time Canadian road race silver medallist Michael Barry competed on the Mont Royal course on two editions of Grand Prix du Cycliste Montreal, when his son was old enough to remember ringing a cowbell at his father's race.

Both parents competed at multiple road world championships for their respective countries; Michael's best effort was eighth in the U23 road race in 1996, while Dede won the junior road title in 1989. And Dede also competed frequently on the track, going fourth at the UCI Junior World Track Championships.

Demet-Barry later translated that speed to a silver medal on the road at the Athens Olympic Games in the individual time trial. An Olympic medal of any colour, and in road or track, has the attention of her son.

Barry said one of the reasons he enjoys the track so much is the emphasis on teamwork, be it Team Pursuit and other events like Madison. In fact, his personal favourite moment from 2025 was not even a win, but a fourth-place finish.

"[Last year] at Track Worlds, we were just off the cusp of getting a medal. But seeing the way that programme's come together has been really cool, and I'm personally proud to be a part of it, proud of those guys and seeing the way they've improved," he said about the US Men's Team Pursuit squad.

"[Track] Worlds will be a really good opportunity for me, and then I'm hoping next year to do Track Worlds again, hoping to get some more racing experience on the track."

This year, the quest for a gold medal in Team Pursuit began on the first day of the 2026 UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai as Barry rejoined Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson with the new addition of Taylor Phinney. They made it through qualifying but not the first round, with France ending their dreams. Barry will race the individual pursuit and Elimination Race later this week.

On the road, before earning his world title, Barry said his top road highlight of the season also showed the teamwork he values.

"There's something special about achieving something with another person or with a group of people, and being able to share that moment. The Olympia story comes to mind. That was just a cool moment, I mean one-two is cool," Barry said about that March race with teammates on the podium.

"We had a great team there. It's a good atmosphere; I really liked that course. I feel proud about the way that I raced there and worked with my teammate Aldo.

"My teammate and I were in that front gro,up and probably we had a pretty equal chance of winning, either one of us. I mean, he was second in the end, but he helped me set up that winning attack. He could have gone to the finish and won. It just ended by luck that I was the one winning."

Barry has the talent, not just the luck. Those two top moments of the past two seasons, however, were probably pushed to runner-up positions after he won the U23 road world championship.

In fact, his personal victory was also one for his country, scoring the country's first-ever U23 world title for a US athlete. And who was the last U23 men's rider to take a medal of any colour? It was his track teammate Taylor Phinney in 2010, who tied Canadian Guillaume Boivin to give the USA a bronze.

items.title: 'Same start time, same distance, same energy' - Charlotte Kool calls out Eneco Tour on unequal prize list
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
However, their focus on equity hasn't made its way to the prize purse, a point that sprint leader Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) pointed out on Instagram. She posted an image of the prize list, which shows the women are racing for a total of €17,205 while the men's purse is €63,465.

"I'm curious if women get a discount at @eneco for energy? Prologue: Same start time, same distance, same energy," Kool wrote in the post.

While men's prologue winner Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) pocketed €1,490 for his effort, women's winner Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) earned just €220. Tim Merlier (Soudal-Quickstep) will take home €3,060 for winning the sprint on stage 1, while Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché) gained just €370.

Speaking to Kool expanded, saying, "It's not about the money for us; that is just a small bonus. It's more about the principle, that it's a bit strange.

"It was a bit of a joke," she said of her post. "Because it is of course a bit skewed that, as the Eneco Tour, you promote that men and women are on equal footing, and then there is such a difference in prize money."

During the 2020 season, Flanders Classics, organisers of the Tour of Flanders and other races, launched an initiative called 'Closing the Gap' to bring more parity to broadcast coverage and prize money. The Tour of Flanders awarded equal prizes in 2022, and Flanders Classics extended that to five other races in 2023.

But events like the Tour de France still give women a tenth of what the men earn, so the fight is not over yet.

items.title: Netcompany Ineos sign 23-year-old former Tour de l'Avenir winner for 2027
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
The young British racer joins Ineos after two years at NSN and Israel-Premier Tech, which followed a dramatically successful 2024 season that saw him win both the Tour de l’Avenir and the U23 Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

This year, however, Blackmore's racing has been severely disrupted by knee injuries, to the point where he took part in just three races and abandoned all of them. He did, however, complete the Tour de France in his first full season as a pro back in 2025, when he also claimed fourth in Brabantse Pijl in the same year.

Blackmore was one of three signings announced by Ineos Grenadiers on Wednesday, the other two being fellow Briton James Shaw and French climber Clément Champoussin.

“I’m extremely excited and grateful for the opportunity to spend the next three years of my career with Netcompany Ineos," Blackmore said in a team press release.

"It’s been a tough 2026 for me with injuries, but it’s made me even more motivated to reach my full potential.

“Joe is a rider we’ve followed closely, and someone we believe has significant potential," Netcompany Ineos director of racing Geraint Thomas added.

"He has already shown what he is capable of across different types of racing, but importantly we believe there is still a lot more to come."

Shaw, 30, has yet to take a win in his career, but with seven Grand Tours in his palmares, the Briton has built a solid reputation as a strong climber. Shaw is also well known for setting his career back on track after two initial pro seasons at Lotto were followed by three away from the WorldTour in smaller squads.

At a point where others would have thrown in the towel, Shaw made it back to the top level and has now raced for the last five years at EF Education-EasyPost. “As a kid, this [Ineos] was the team that inspired me," Shaw said.

"I grew up looking up to riders like Geraint Thomas, so to now have the opportunity to pull on the jersey and become part of a team I've admired for so long is a dream come true."

Also set to provide a boost to Netcompany Ineos climbing line-up in 2027, like Shaw, is 28-year-old Clément Champoussin, moving on from XDS-Astana to race with the British WorldTour team next season.

A former top-ten finisher in Paris-Nice and Itzulia Basque Country, Champoussin has signed a three-year deal through to 2029 with Netcompany Ineos. They will be his fourth professional team following spells as AG2R-Decathlon, Arkéa-Samsic and, most recently, two years at Astana.

This year a promising early start for Champoussin, including a fifth place overall at Itzulia Basque Country and top 20 placings in La Flèche Wallonne and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, was followed by a more uneven midseason. 2026 was the first time since 2022 that the Frenchman has not taken part in a single Grand Tour, where his best placing remains 16th overall in the Vuelta back in 2021.

“Clément brings significant experience and another dimension to the group," Thomas added about the Frenchman, originally from Nice, but now reportedly a resident in Andorra.

"He's a solid, strong and consistent climber who has shown he can perform at the highest level.

In a busy transfer season for Netcompany Ineos, the British squad is set to see multiple significant departures and arrivals this winter. Amongst those departing are Italian time trial giant Filippo Ganna, Americans AJ August and Magnus Sheffield, British allrounder Ben Swift, who is retiring, and Australian sprinter Sam Welsford.

Meanwhile, Champoussin, Shaw and Blackmore are three of the seven riders currently confirmed to be heading the opposite direction, with others joining Ineos including Champoussin's current XDS-Astana teammate, Harold Tejada, and the teenage Spanish star and double junior World Champion, Benjamin Noval.

items.title: 'I was deliberately pushed into the barriers' – Guarischi relegated from Eneco Tour sprint after complaints from Kool
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Barbara Guarischi (SD Worx-Protime) has been relegated for her sprint on stage 1 of the Eneco Tour, after her actions left Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech), the rider she hampered in the final 150 metres, furious at the finish line on Wednesday.

Kool was the favourite for the flat stage in Ede, and was well placed on the wheel of the Italian rider coming out of the final corner. As Guarischi launched her sprint in the middle of the road, Kool began to launch on her left, only for the Italian rider to close her to the barrier, causing the Dutch rider to take evasive action and restart her sprint on the other side.

By the time she was back up to speed, Kool had already lost the stage to Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché), turning back and throwing her hand in the air at Guarischi for her actions in the sprint. Kool didn't mince her words when she spoke after the stage.

"I'm just really bummed that as a team we're sacrificing everything to let it come down to a sprint; you just want a fair chance," said Kool to Dutch publication .

"I think that fair chance has been taken away from me now. I find that very unsportsmanlike and very unfortunate.

"I haven't seen it back yet, but in my view, I was deliberately and intentionally pushed into the barriers. It wasn't just a little bit of a deviation from the line; it went from right to left. So yes, I find that very unsportsmanlike.

"Everyone knows images from the past. That goes through your head. I really want to win, but not much. And I also know that she won't give up easily, because she didn't do that to begin with."

The official results initially showed no consequences for Guarischi's sprint, but a post on AG Insurance Soudal's social media pages later on Wednesday evening confirmed that the Italian had been relegated, putting her at the back of the bunch in 85th.

"Nicola Steigenga has been promoted to third place in the final race classification of the first stage, following a race incident and the subsequent disqualification of the rider initially classified in third place," read a post from AG Insurance Soudal.

While the results page on the Eneco Tour's website has, at the time of writing, not been updated with the relegation for Guarischi, it is likely she was deemed to have broken rule 2.3.036 of the UCI regulations: "Riders shall be strictly forbidden to deviate from the lane they selected when launching into the sprint and, in so doing, obstructing or endangering others."

items.title: Taylor Phinney's return from retirement in UCI Track World Championships fizzles as US men miss finals in team pursuit
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
The highly-anticipated return of 2010 pursuit world champion Taylor Phinney to international competition at the UCI Track World Championships as the starter for Team USA's men's team pursuit squad ended on day 1, the quartet missing the medal finals. It's a step backward for the team, who finished fourth in last year's championships in Santiago, Chile.

Phinney made a late decision to join the USA Cycling programme, announcing his return in April, more than six years after he quit professional cycling at age 29 in 2019. His aim was to make the team for the Los Angeles Olympic Games to emulate his parents Davis Phinney and Connie Carpenter-Phinney, who both earned medals at the last Olympics there in 1984.

"The track was where I first found love and success in this sport, it was even the first discipline to break my heart when my specialty event, the individual pursuit, was removed from the Olympic programme, which prompted me to swiftly abandon the track and go all in on the road," Phinney wrote in April.

"Recently, the USA boys have been making huge strides in the Team Pursuit, and I couldn't be more stoked to be joining them in the chase for the Olympic Dream."

Phinney joined Ashlin Barry, Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson for the Team Pursuit on Wednesday, stepping in for last year's team member Graeme Frislie, who will compete in the Omnium, Madison and Scratch Race.

Speaking to the UCI on Wednesday before racing started in the Shanghai Velodrome on Chongming Island, Phinney said being back at the highest level on the track "feels like coming home in a lot of ways".

"It's really fun to ride with the guys," he said. "The technology has changed quite a lot, especially in team pursuiting.

"The positions have changed a lot. If you look at my position in the individual pursuit from 2009 - it was like completely wide open, and now everything is super close. So I think the position is more extreme, but the power numbers, they are not like so much different.

"I'm also racing as the starter, so I take a lot of the first minute of the race, getting everybody up to speed. I mean, we have a really strong team. It's kind of a question mark coming into the race, trying to understand where the other teams are at."

Phinney was realistic about the team's chances, saying before the race: "If we could do a top five, I think we would be really happy with that. And if we go into the finals, then we are more than stoked. But we'll take it one every one round at a time."

While the team did enough in the qualifying round to move on to the next heat, which determined the teams for the medal finals, they were unable to advance, setting times two seconds slower than the team did in 2025 and missing the medal round by half a second.

items.title: Red Bull's F1 boss gets well-timed endorsement with extended deal
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Red Bull has given a very strong endorsement of Laurent Mekies' leadership by publicly announcing the extension of his contract as its Formula 1 team principal through 2031.

Though it is increasingly common for F1 team principals both to be on specific-term contracts rather than rolling employee deals, and for extensions of those deals to be announced in public, Red Bull's strong display of faith in Mekies still stands out as a message the company hierarchy clearly wanted the world to hear.

He was swiftly moved across from junior team Racing Bulls when Christian Horner was ousted from Red Bull last summer.

The Red Bull press release announcing Mekies’ new deal specifically highlighted that "under Laurent’s leadership, the team delivered a remarkable turnaround during the second half of the 2025 season, ultimately missing out on the drivers’ championship by just two points".

The announcement of Mekies’ new deal comes after Max Verstappen’s decision to commit to Red Bull for the long term, the team extending Isack Hadjar’s deal, and Verstappen taking back to back wins in Malaysia and Singapore.

It also coincides with Mekies’ predecessor Horner being back in the public eye around the launch of his new book and an associated run of interviews in which his time at - and exit from - Red Bull are a major topic.

A joint comment from Red Bull shareholders Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz read: "Laurent has played a crucial role in guiding the team through an important period of transition while maintaining the competitive spirit and the Red Bull principles that define us.

"This extension reflects our confidence in his leadership and our shared belief in the long-term vision of the team."

items.title: What to expect from WEC's Barcelona debut
'We have been in touch with the rider directly and apologised' – ITA responds to Valentina Cavallar's post about doping control on day her mother died
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The International Testing Agency (ITA) have apologised to Austrian rider Valentina Cavallar after an anti-doping officer arrived to test her following the death of her mother, while at the same time defending their procedures.

A doping control officer arrived at Cavallar's home "just a few hours" after her mother's death in September, she wrote, and the test was carried out with her mother in the next room.

"It was a moment that made me reflect on how easily we can forget that behind every athlete, there is a human being with a life, a family and emotions that do not simply disappear when the responsibilities of professional sport begin," added the SD Worx-Protime racer.

The ITA stated that Cavallar informed the doping control officer of her mother's death shortly after their arrival, but noted that she raised "no concerns or requests to postpone or discontinue the control" at the time.

"The International Testing Agency (ITA) extends its sincere condolences to Valentina Cavallar and her family following the loss of her mother," the statement to read.

"Since learning about the circumstances of the sample collection which took place on 5 September 2026 on Valentina Cavallar, the ITA looked into the context of the test.

"Neither the ITA nor the Doping Control Officer (DCO) were aware of the rider’s personal situation prior to arriving at her home. The DCO was informed of her mother’s passing upon arrival. According to the information gathered by the ITA since the rider’s Instagram post [Monday], Ms Cavallar and her family cooperated fully with the procedure, and no concerns or requests to postpone or discontinue the control were raised at the time or afterwards."

Under cycling's whereabouts system, riders must submit their location during a 60-minute period each day when they will be available for testing. Cavallar's situation occurred was a result of tragic coincidence, which the ITA acknowledged as an "exceptionally sensitive situation."

The doping control officer "endeavoured to pursue the procedure as discreetly, respectfully and swiftly as possible" with Cavallar and her family's support, the ITA's statement continued, before the organisation noted that it had reached out to her to apologise directly for the situation and any distress caused.

"We fully recognise that undergoing a doping control in these circumstances has added to her distress experienced at an extraordinarily painful time. We have been in touch with the rider directly and apologised.

"The ITA remains committed to ensuring that the protection of clean sport goes hand in hand with respect, compassion and care for athletes.

"We will also continue to always encourage athletes to report any concerns either during or after a doping control, so the ITA can take the appropriate measures to ensure a proportionate balance between the fight against doping and every athlete’s right to privacy and wellbeing."

items.title: Car enters course during Dutch race just four days after rider safety protest at Il Lombardia
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
A driver entered Wednesday's race route with around 70km to go just ahead of the breakaway, going in the same direction. Fortunately an in-race marshal was able to direct the green car to the side of the road from a motorbike, where it pulled over, allowing the three breakaway riders to pass safely.

Thankfully, the peloton were 1:44 behind, so by the time they reached the spot where the car was, it had already been diverted off the course. But it's the latest in a run of incidents which forced the riders' hands before the last Monument of the season.

Remco Evenepoel led the protest and delayed start in Italy on Saturday, giving a speech in which he said: "We want to make this statement because there's too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race. Unfortunately we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us, so we want to make this statement to show to the world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying in what we like the most to do."

Since his death, non-race vehicles have entered the route at the Giro dell'Emilia and Coppa Bernocchi, with a police motorbike going the wrong way during Tre Valli Varesine also knocking two of Tom Pidcock's Pinarello Q36.5 teammates out of the race.

Racing continued on Wednesday with Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) taking the win on the impacted Eneco Tour stage, but it's the latest in a run of shocking incidents just this year which forced the riders to take a stand at Il Lombardia.

At the same time as Evenepoel spoke, a scheduled shared statement was released by many of the riders in the professional peloton, in which they called for action from cycling's governing body, the UCI, and race organisers.

"As riders, we stand united against the unnecessary risk our lives are being subjected to," it read.

"[Last] week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses. Two riders crashed when they hit a motorbike who was driving the wrong way on the race route. Luckily both escaped with cuts and bruises, it could have been so much worse.

"This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer. Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the UCI and race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met.

"We are calling for the UCI and race organisers to take accountability and act. That means a serious, open conversation between riders, race organisers and the UCI resulting in concrete changes to how race routes are secured and managed.

"After five minutes, we raced as normal. We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one. We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones."

items.title: Giro del Veneto: Alessandro Covi pulls off first win of 2026 with well-timed sprint
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
An exceptionally long uphill drive for the line netted Jayco-AlUla racer Alessandro Covi a small bunch sprint victory on home soil in the Giro del Veneto on Wednesday.

Covi began his move some 300 metres to go on Vicenza's Monte Berico, and the Italian climber narrowly fended off a almost equally persistent Uno-X Mobility's Anthon Charmig to claim his first victory since a stage of the Vuelta a Asturias last year.

UAE Team Emirates-XRG had dominated proceedings in a tightly controlled bunch in the last 50 kilometres, first with Pavel Sivakov and then with World Champion Brandon McNulty. But their designated contender, France's Benoit Cosnefrôy, could not repeat teammate Isaac del Toro's win in Veneto last year and finally had to settle for third.

Covi's home triumph also ended a lengthy drought on victories for Jayco-AlUla, whose last win was a stage of 2026 Tour de France with Mauro Schmid.

Asked by race TV about his lengthy wait for a victory this year with Jayco-AlUla, Covi explained that it was impossible to predict when success would happen.

"You never know, it's difficult to win, but if it happens in October it's still a big victory," he said.

"Also, it's a nice race, I already did it a few times. It's the end of the season, a lot of the guys are tired - me too.

"But it's nice to win with a new jersey, [it's been] ten months before this victory arrived but it's a really nice victory."

In a race which took a long time to come alive, an early attack by eight low-profile riders, all of them from Continental or Club level bar one, Tommaso Nencini (Solution Tech Nippo Rali), was the standout feature of the first 100 kilometres.

Together with Nencini, the strongest in the all-Italian break - Francisco Carollo and his Swatt Club teammate, Giacomo Garavaglia , Kevin Pezzo Rosola and Thomas Rossetti (both General Store - Essegibi - F.Lli Curia), Leonardo Volpato (Campana Imballaggi - Morbiato - Trentino) and Riccardo Lorello (S.C. Padovani Polo Cherry Bank) had a two-minute lead on the pack as they passed the finish line for the first time in Vicenza, positioned two thirds of the way up the kilometre-long Monte Berico.

Having enjoyed their time in the warm autumn sunshine, with three local laps of five and 44 kilometres to go the last of the early breakaways was caught, in large part thanks to Pavel Sivakov's aggressive patrolling on the front of the bunch. Whilst a subsequent brief dig by Andrea Petrobon (Polti-VisitMalta) kept viewers entertained, there was little sense, though, that the main contenders were ready - or perhaps even able, given UAE's iron grip on proceedings - to make a long-distance move.

Once Petrobon was sucked in on the second-to-last ascent of the Monte Berico, the same grinding-down process continued, as UAE both controlled their most dangerous rivals with a high pace that simultaneously saw numerous riders shed out the back.

Pounding up the Arcugnano, the other, far gentler, main ascent on the circuit, Sivakov kept up the hard work whilst the white jersey of teammate and World Champion Brandon McNulty was never far away, either.

Tudor and Uno-X Mobility were the keenest to lead into the last full ascent of the Berico, but their efforts to break UAE's long stranglehold on affairs proved limited. Rather, Sivakov delivered one final effort, and as the bunch romped through the finish line and over the top of the grinding, steady climb, McNulty himself tried to go clear.

The American's flick-of-the-elbow gesture to co-attacker Christian Scaroni (XDS-Astana) to come through failed to spark enough of a reaction, though for his plan to work out, and instead there was a general regrouping. Marc Hirschi (Tudor) then rolled back the years with a searing uphill move, and while McNulty visibly sat up, both Hirschi and Fabio Christen (Pinarello-Q36.5) were able to go clear.

The two had a gap of almost ten seconds as they blasted along the undulating Arcugnano and McNulty then delivered yet another counter-attack to try and bridge across. However, the American could not make it alone, his rainbow jersey meaning he was heavily marked.

Even so, with six kilometres to go McNulty's constant accelerations did bring the bunch up to the two Swiss riders, and the American then almost single handedly ensured things remained together en route to the final, partial ascent of the Berico.

The front group of some 60 or 70 riders was still loosely together on the foot of the climb, as McNulty continued to drive away, only dropping back with 400 metres to go. However, Covi then launched a very long, sustained acceleration that saw the Italian both draw out the main group and stay ahead. Then whilst Charmig pushed Covi hard and Cosnefrôy and Christen were closing in fast, the 28-year-old Italian still had both the energy and resistance to manage to keep his rivals behind his front wheel all the way to the line.

"[Teammate Andrea] Vendrame was the guy we had for the sprint, but in the middle of the circuit, he came to me, said he didn't feel good and I should wait for the sprint," Covi explained afterwards about how he'd taken a much-needed victory for himself and the team.

"So I did exactly what he said, I never moved, I was always in the first group and I just tried for the sprint, and then I won. So that was super nice of Andrea, too."

items.title: Eneco Tour: Tim Merlier wins stage 1 sprint in Ede ahead of Dylan Groenewegen
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) sailed to victory on stage 1 at Eneco Tour launching a long-range sprint on the final 400 metres which had no reply from rivals.

Dylan Groenewegen (Unibet Rose Rockets) trailed in second while Gerben Thijssen (Alpecin-Premier Tech) took third ahead of Visma-Lease a Bike's Christophe Laporte.

The win moved Merlier 27 positions in the GC standings, now fifth overall. The top four positions held firm with just a two-second gap established from the opening prologue, Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) in the leader's jersey. Wessel Mouris (Unibet Rose Rockets) remains in second place, Laporte in third and Merlier's teammate Ethan Hayter in fourth.

Once at the flamme rouge, Soudal-QuickStep went into formation for Merlier on the right side of the course. At the final 90-degree corner with 400 metres to go, Nils Eekhoff from Picnic PostNL took the lead with riders from Unibet Rose Rockets, Visma-Lease a Bike and Alpecin just behind. Merlier exploded past them all and won by several bike lengths.

"It was quite hectic [in the final kilometre], and then we speed up, a really high speed. It was also difficult to find each other, but in the end we did really well," Merlier said about scoring his 13th victory on Wednesday.

"They bring me to a good position, and then I choose what I'm gonna do in the last 500 metres. I think it was a bit of a risk to go a bit further, but in the end, I can go in the slipstream, and speed up from behind the other guys. This kind of finish suits me really well."

After the 3.1km prologue to set the leaderboard, stage 1 took place with a flat 40-kilometre circuit on the north side of Ede tackled three times for 120km.

The peloton began the opening kilometres sizing up each other under the sunny skies, with the seven WorldTour teams massing at the front. Then a trio from a Dutch Continental squads were allowed to accelerate away - Johan Dorussen (Metec-SOLARWATT p/b Mantel), Rick Ottema (EEW-VDK Cyclingteam) and Luke Verburg (Azerion-Villa Valkenburg). .

Once on the second circuit, the three riders took shares in maintaining their breakaway and built a gap of 3:00. On the approach to Ede for the final loop, the gap began to fade as the peloton sensed time to position their fast men.

The breakaway trio scooped up all the bonuses at the intermediate sprint with 24km to go, but the peloton was only 15 seconds back with 15km to go. A wall of sprint teams, led by Soudal-QuickStep, Picnic PostNL and Unibet Rose Rockets, spread across the road and charged from behind to end the breakaway with 11km to go.

As the shadows began to stretch across the road with the sun beginning to fade in late afternoon, the peloton seemed to settle down on the next four kilometres heading back into the city limits. Visma-Lease a Bike edged to the front to support Christophe Laporte alongside Soudal-QuickStep while Unibet Rose Rockets held position on an outside line for Wessel Mouris with Lotto-Intermarché sending riders up. Lidl-Trek was there for race leader Jakob Söderqvist, biding their time as the finish neared.

It wasn't until 2km to go that the wide procession began to fracture, Soudal-QuickStep amping up the action. This straight run led to a defining sharp left-hand corner onto Arnhemseweg for the final 400 metres.

On that final corner, Merlier used the slipstream of his teammate Bert Van Lerberghe to vault from sixth position to first as he flew down the straightaway for the victory.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Stay diligent’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Four of the five Knicks starters didn’t board a plane north of the border, the fifth one didn’t play basketball on Tuesday, and it all showed badly.

New York will host a preseason game for one final time on Thursday before dressing in gold for Tuesday’s banner night.

Here’s the latest from Mike, James, and Miles.

On the Knicks’ performance and defensive shortcomings in their 50-point preseason loss to Toronto:

“It’s not necessarily what’s on the scoreboard at that particular time. It is: are you doing the right things to be better and/or get better? And in the first half, what I was most disappointed in was we weren’t putting bodies on bodies. Fifteen second-chance points in one half is not good. Thirty fast-break points in one half is not good.

“And then the way they sped us up, and us not necessarily touching the paint and trying to spray it and/or making quick decisions is not good. So that’s what I was most disappointed in in the first half. I really didn’t care about the score, especially with the group we had on the floor.”

On how James Wiseman has developed since his time with the Warriors:

“Back then, obviously, he was talented but he was really raw in terms of his ability and feel on the court. It’s obviously a lot higher now, but he’s also been humbled a little bit with the challenges and the adversity he’s gone through in his career. He understands how hard it is. That obviously is different now than what it was back then.”

On Wiseman’s growth and understanding of how quickly NBA opportunities can disappear:

“Everything was new to him. He was a wide-eyed young puppy and now he’s a little bit more seasoned with the knowledge of, ‘This is not gonna be easy and opportunities can come and go like that.’”

On appreciating his opportunity to compete for a roster spot with the Knicks:

“It’s a blessing to just be here. Really just being able to go out there, enjoy myself, have fun, just keep working. Stay diligent.”

On overcoming injuries and adversity throughout his NBA career:

“It’s been a lot. Really just putting God first. Staying down, grinding every single day and just taking one day at a time. That’s really all you can do, just really control what you can.”

On what he has learned about himself through his career struggles:

“Really just being able to stay resilient through the process and really just staying persistent as well.”

On how his athleticism can help him earn the Knicks’ final roster spot:

“Just being able to use my athleticism. Being able to put my head on the rim every single time, run the floor and really just being vocal.”

On the Knicks’ 50-point preseason loss to the Raptors:

“You never want to lose in that way. But at the same time, we just gotta move on. Preseason is for those reasons. Missing eight of our guys, you just want to come out there and have a positive mindset. Go out there and play hard. There were things we could’ve definitely done better, but they’re a playoff team and you add a Hall of Famer with them.”

items.title: Track World Championships: Lorena Wiebes triumphs again in scratch race, Taylor Phinney returns with USA team pursuit squad
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
As was the case last year, rainbow jerseys were awarded for the women's scratch race and both the men's and women's team sprints, while qualification rounds for the men's and women's team pursuits came earlier in the day.

Lorena Wiebes scored the first gold of the Championships in the women's scratch race, while the Netherlands won the men's team sprint for the third year in succession and the home nation triumphed in the women's team sprint.

Read on for full reports and results from all of Wednesday's action.

Dutch star Lorena Wiebes took home the first rainbow jersey of the week, but only just, as she prevailed for the third year in a row at the scratch race. At the line, Wiebes edged out Lara Gillespie by centimetres to hang on and win as the Irishwoman launched from behind to take silver.

The 40-lap race saw a host of riders sweep to the front and up the pace as Wiebes' rivals sought to throw her off her stride ahead of the final. She lay in wait further back, comfortable in her position as she waited for the closing sprint.

After 10 minutes of racing, the riders reached the final 10 laps, with no big move at the front. With seven laps to go, France's Valentine Fortin leapt first as Wiebes jumped from the group to chase.

A regrouping followed as Wiebes dropped back again, and Belgium's Hélène Hesters led it into the final four laps. Wiebes came back, though, coming around the outside to hit the front again with two laps to go.

Gillespie was on her wheel, taking Portugal's Maria Martins with her as the lead trio opened up a gap on the rest on the final lap. Wiebes led around the final bend, but faded in the final metres before the line. Gillespie closed in but just missed out on passing the Dutchwoman, while Martins finished just behind the pair to take bronze.

"I think it's quite crazy. Of course you always go for the win, but it's always harder and harder to repeat it. Today was also really close. Lara came really close, but it was enough to win, and that's all I need," Wiebes said after her triumph.

"I think at the end, I needed to start my sprint a bit too early, but you also need to adapt to that situation, and I tried as good as possible. Lara was also really fast today, but I'm happy it was enough. That's the thing with scratch racing; it's also about positioning and tactics, not only the speed in the legs."

The Netherlands (Jeffrey Hoogland, Harrie Lavreysen, Roy van den Berg), reigning world champions and unbeaten in this event since 2023, re-established themselves as favourites in the qualifying and first rounds, going quickest at both to sweep into the final round.

Australia (Daniel Barber, Ryan Elliott, Leigh Hoffman) ran them close, though, heading into the gold medal race with a mere 0.115-second deficit after improving on their qualifying run.

China (Zhiheng Jin, Zhiwei Li, Qi Liu) and Japan (Yoshitaku Nagasako, Minato Nakaishi, Kaiya Ota), second and third in the qualifying round, completed the top four in the first round, both coming through with a near-0.2-second gap to fifth-placed Trinidad and Tobago.

In the final, China and Japan battled for bronze, and the home nation had the upper hand early on. They passed the 250-metre mark 0.035 seconds up on Japan, who looked less organised from the start, with a rider dropping behind. China duly capitalised on that error to race to a 0.947-second advantage after 625 metres, and they finished it off to win bronze, 1.255 seconds ahead of Japan.

In the gold medal race, it was reigning world champions, the Netherlands, versus last year's bronze medallists, Australia. The Dutch slipped behind early on, though, losing 0.219 seconds in the opening 250 metres, but they closed it to almost a dead heat over the next 250, starting the final run just 0.005 seconds off their rivals. A tense closing 250 metres saw the Dutch turn it around to win the rainbow jersey once again, finishing the race 0.516 seconds quicker than silver medallists Australia.

"It's an amazing feeling. I've got seven world titles, and they've got eight. It means a lot. We've been training very hard the last year, and when everything comes together at the most important race, it's amazing," said Van den Berg, before Hoogland described the final push in the race.

"I was just mad going into the final, so I gave it my all in the last lap. I threw everything I knew out of the window and just started pushing the pedals," he said.

Lavreysen said he was happy to win again after a long drought for the team, saying, "I'm very happy we can start the [Olympic] qualification with a win. We didn't win any races since last World Championships, so I'm really happy we can keep the jersey and show it this year."

There were few surprises in the qualifying round of the women's team sprint as the major nations progressed, with Great Britain (Sophie Capewell, Emma Finucane, Rhianna Parris-Smith) and China (Yulu Jiang, Mengqi Tong, Liying Yuan) leading the way at each stage.

The two nations made it through the first round, with China on top by 0.280 seconds as Germany (Lea Friedrich, Pauline Grabosch, Clara Schneider) and the Individual Neutral Athletes (Iana Burlakova, Ekaterina Evlanova, Alina Lysenko) finished with the third- and fourth-best times to make the battle for bronze.

One major surprise in the first round came as the reigning champions, the Netherlands (Kimberley Kalee, Hetty van de Wouw, Steffie van der Peet), missed out on the final, finishing fifth, 0.048 seconds off fourth place.

In the bronze medal race, Germany started slow, losing 0.310 seconds to the Individual Neutral Athletes in the first 250 metres. They gradually turned things around, though, closing to 0.172 seconds down after 500 metres as the final riders faced off. It was Germany who prevailed, however, riding a big final leg to turn that deficit into a 0.436-second advantage at the finish line to take the medal.

Great Britain and China faced off in the gold medal race, and it was the British who landed the first blow, completing the opening 250 metres 0.172 seconds quicker.

China fought back, though, with the pendulum swinging to 0.347 seconds in their favour after 500 metres. They duly held the advantage over the closing leg to win the rainbow jerseys with a 0.355-second gap over Great Britain, who finished with a silver medal for the second year in a row.

items.title: Shopping for a kids' bike before Christmas? Now is the time to grab up to 60% off top brands at Evans Cycles
items.author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
items.content:
With Christmas right around the corner, now is the ideal time to pick up a discounted kids' bike. Many online cycling retailers and bike brands are already offering fantastic deals on some of the best children's bikes as the countdown to Christmas begins.

Evans Cycles has some real eye-catching deals with up to 60% off when you use the code KIDS20 at checkout. It's only on selected bikes, but includes models from leading kids' brands like Frog and Pinnacle. Evans has plenty of others on sale too, carrying worthy reductions.

Gifting a child their first real bike builds memories and can spark a lifelong love for cycling, or even produce the next Brandon McNulty or Demi Vollering. Scoring the best possible bike at a great price makes the experience even better. Read on for my top kids' bike deals, plus essential buying advice to help you choose the right model.

Gravel 67 26-Inch Kids Bike
Track 67 24-Inch Kids Bike

Kids' bikes have come a long way since the days of my much loved Raleigh Burner. Today’s youth bikes mirror adult models in geometry, components, and capability. If you want your child to join you on some proper rides, their setup needs to keep up with yours. To help you navigate the endless options, here are a few key factors to consider.

Getting the right size bike is crucial for a child's safety and confidence, an awkward fit can easily ruin the fun. Since kids grow fast, rely on the brand's age, height, and inseam guides to find the sweet spot, especially when ordering online. If you can visit a local bike shop, test the fit in person: for younger/new riders your child should comfortably touch the ground with both feet from the saddle and reach the handlebars, brake levers, and shifters without straining.

Weight matters even more for children than it does for adults. A heavy, cumbersome bike is exhausting to maneuver and can quickly turn a fun ride into a struggle. Aim for the lightest your budget allows. While most brands publish bike weights online, testing models in-store makes it easy to compare weight in person before buying.

The bikes featured above deliver excellent build quality at a discounted price, giving you maximum value for your money. When setting your budget, factor in room for growth alongside essentials like one of the best kids' helmets, and some proper riding gear, and again speaking from experience here, looking good is most important.

Never underestimate the importance of looks, to a child, colour and style often matter far more than components or specs. Involve them in the final pick before pulling the trigger, or you risk leaving an unwanted bike sitting in the garage. And if you're passing down a sibling's old ride, a few fresh grips or decals can go a long way in making it feel like theirs.

Former Zwift Academy winner Emily Dixon moves up to Canyon-SRAM WorldTour team
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Promising young Australian rider Emily Dixon has been confirmed as part of the Canyon-SRAM WorldTour team for the next two seasons.

A former Zwift Academy winner back in 2024, Dixon has been racing for the last two years with the Canyon-SRAM Generation squad. She will now make a further key move in her career, into Canyon's top racing team.

Twelfth in the 2026 under-23 women's World Championships road race and the winner of two stages in the Gracia Orlová race back in April, also leading it for several days, Dixon has shown considerable promise this season. Her consistency in longer events was on display, too, when she took third in the toughest stage of the Tour Féminin International des Pyrénées, finally ending sixth overall and second in the BYR rankings.

Dixon will now make the senior Canyon-SRAM WorldTour team her squad for 2027. That's just two years after she beat more than 100,000 other contenders for a Continental contract with Canyon-SRAM Generation, confirmed in March 2025, and before she has reached 20.

"They say ‘never stop dreaming’, and one dream was to be in Europe racing for a pretty cool team like Canyon-SRAM," Dixon said in a press release.

"Now, it’s another dream coming true to race for the WorldTeam. I didn’t think this would be possible before turning 20, so I think my younger self would be very proud.

"I knew when signing with Generation that WorldTour was what I wanted, but I wasn’t so satisfied with my 2025 season and didn’t quite expect to make the jump I have this year.

"So, in a way, I’ve surprised myself, and that’s why I’m a bit like, ‘Whoa, I’m signing WorldTour.’ I’m really happy with my progression."

"The team recognises that she’s a young rider, and I believe it’s good that she will be moving to WorldTour level in the same organisation," added Generation Team Manager and Sports Director Gosia Jasinska in the same press release.

"I’ve already talked with the WorldTeam sport directors, and they’ve also worked with her already, so they know it’s not necessary to put pressure on her shoulders because she’s the kind of person who is already hard on herself.

"In her first year at least, it will be a big step to ride in the WorldTour, but I think racing amongst the top names and for strong leaders will be a pleasure and very fun for her. Still, I think she could definitely find some opportunities for herself."

Discussing her move to senior level in Canyon-SRAM and how it came about, Dixon added that "I think what’s changed has been my mindset."

"And that seems really cliché, but I think for the road race at [the Australian] Nationals" - taking sixth on the day behind Mackenzie Coupland - "I really focused on my mentality as I realised how much my mind would affect my racing. That road race proved it to me and kind of unlocked the power of my mind, which has really helped me this year, especially with positioning.

As for 2027 and her first season at WorldTour level, she said: "I want to be a really good teammate – that sounds a little bit stupid, but I really want to be there for the team.

"I want to go to the races and do exactly what I’ve been asked to do. I also want to be in a team that succeeds, and Canyon-SRAM does that very well, so I’d love to be part of that atmosphere while learning from everyone much more experienced than me.

"I’m very keen to put on the WorldTeam jersey and for it to actually be mine – that’s so cool! It will say WorldTour, and that’s been my dream, and it’s actually going to be real."

items.title: Veneto Women: Liane Lippert rounds out 2026 season with solo summit victory in Italy
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
The final one-day race of the 2026 elite women's season, Veneto Women, has been captured by German allrounder Liane Lippert (Movistar) in a late solo charge for the line.

Lippert roared home atop the short but punishing final ascent of Monte Berico in the northern Italian city of Vicenza, four seconds clear of closest pursuer Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek). Local favourite Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD) finished six seconds back.

After a flurry of early attacks, the race situation calmed down considerably, with Uno-X Mobility doing most of the work. More than half the total 106-kilometre distance had passed before a move of half a dozen riders managed to claw its way clear, the dangerous attack including the 2026 Trofeo Alfredo Binda and Giro dell'Emilia winners, Karlijn Swinkels (UAE Team L'IMAD) and Alessia Vigilia (Uno-X Mobility).

However, Movistar and Lidl-Trek ensured they never got more than 35 seconds advantage, and with 20 kilometres to go, the peloton was still compact, albeit fast shedding riders from the back on the relentlessly hilly finale.

Finally, another dangerous move emerged shortly after the second and final descent of the Arcugnano climb, this time containing Italian National Champion Longo Borghini and no less than three of her teammates in a group of eight - Mavi García, Eleonora Gasparrini and Swinkels. At the same time, Movistar were also well represented with Marlen Reusser, second last year ahead of Gasparrini, and her teammate Lippert. Also present were Noemi Ruegg (EF Education-Oatly) and Adegeest.

With a 30-second advantage in the final five kilometres, it was clear one of the eight would claim the victory in the penultimate race of the 2026 women's calendar. Ultimately, Lippert was able to claim her first triumph of the season since the

Vuelta CV Féminas one-day race, all the way back in February, again with a late solo move.

items.title: TotalEnergies future still hangs in the balance as initial teams registration deadline of October 15 looms
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
The October 15 deadline for teams to make their registration for the 2027 season is approaching fast, but longstanding French ProTeam squad TotalEnergies have yet to issue a definitive statement about the viability of their future for next year.

The lack of recent updates means the uncertainty surrounding the future of TotalEnergies, formed back in 2000 as the Bonjour squad but seemingly still on the hunt for new financial backers for 2027, is set to continue, at least in the short term

According to, although team bosses Stéphane Heulot and Jean-René Bernaudeau have said over the last few months that they remain confident and are working on finding a sponsor, more than a third of the current 28-rider lineup have either signed elsewhere or announced they will be retiring.

Amongst those higher-profile riders leaving are Jordan Jegat, tenth overall in the Tour de France in 2025 and 2026, who is heading to Lidl-Trek, whilst TotalEnergies teammate Geoffrey Bouchard, a former mountains classification winner in both the Vuelta a España and the Giro d'Italia, is ending his career.

also report that no statement updating the team's future is planned before Thursday's initial registration deadline. After October 15, teams can still register, but only if they pay a daily financial penalty and prove a percentage of riders are under contract for the following season.

There are also rumours that in 2027 TotalEnergies may revert to Continental status in a new iteration of Vendée U, its current feeder team, according to

TotalEnergies are far from being the only leading men's Proteam either with a large question mark looming over their future or already definitively ending after this year.

items.title: Eneco Tour Women: Sandrine Tas storms to stage 1 victory as runner-up Charlotte Kool fumes after being hampered in sprint
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Olympic speed skater Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché) stormed to her third professional cycling victory on stage 1 of the 2026 Eneco Tour Women, beating Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) with a powerful sprint in Ede on Wednesday.

Kool threw her hands in the air and complained as she crossed the line, after trying to sprint from the wheel of Barbara Guarischi (SD Worx-ProTime) but getting squeezed by the Italian towards the barriers, and having to restart her final effort.

Opting for a different lane, Tas slingshotted to victory out of the slipstream of the two riders from the breakaway, Talia Appleton (Liv AlUla Jayco) and Fariba Hashimi (Vini Fantini-BePink), who survived into the final 250 metres until they were reeled in by the bunch.

Thanks to her fourth-place finish in Tuesday night's prologue, Tas moved into the overall lead of the Eneco Tour with the winning bonus seconds, one second ahead of prologue winner Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike), and three seconds ahead of Kool.

"First of all, my team did a perfect job positioning me for the last corner, so I knew I was in the right wheel," said a delighted Tas.

"When I saw they started the sprint on the left, I just went full on the right. It was quite a tough sprint; a little bit uphill, and I knew I just had to keep pushing even if lactic acid was everywhere, and I am so happy I managed to finish off the work of my team.

"Actually, I was in the wheel of Charlotte [Kool] in the last corner, but then in the end, I always like to do my own thing, find my own line, and it worked out perfectly this time."

She'll look to defend the leader's orange jersey on stage 2, another race against the clock. This time, it will be a 13.6km flat individual time trial route in Tilburg which decides the victory.

items.title: 'I understand the seriousness of what has been raised' – Matthew Richardson issues statement after removal from Great Britain's Track Worlds squad
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
After British Cycling withdrew Matthew Richardson from the Track World Championships, the racer has issued an Instagram statement saying he will cooperate with the organisation's investigation.

Richardson was sent home from China, where the Track Worlds are ongoing in Shanghai, and he left Harry Ledingham-Horn, Ed Lowe and Joe Truman to compete in Great Britain's men's team sprint lineup.

On Tuesday, Richardson posted a statement on Instagram about the investigation.

"I understand the seriousness of what has been raised in recent reports about my withdrawal from the 2026 UCI Track Cycling World Championships," he wrote.

"British Cycling has said it looks into matters like this through its established procedures. I will co-operate fully with its processes. I assure everyone that I will do so properly, and appropriately and with contrition for the feelings of anyone who might be affected.

"Out of fairness to everyone involved, and on advice, like British Cycling, I will not be commenting further until any process is complete. I am deeply disappointed to miss the World Championships, and I wish the Great Britain team and every rider competing the very best.

"I ask that my family’s privacy is respected at this time."

Last week, British Cycling told The Times that "British Cycling takes any allegations of harassment, bullying or discrimination extremely seriously.

"Where concerns are raised, they are investigated thoroughly through our established procedures. Out of fairness to anyone involved in an investigation, we would not comment on any ongoing process."

Richardson, who had previously raced for Australia before switching nations, was among the medal hopefuls on the Great Britain team, having taken silver medals in the team sprint and individual sprint competitions in Chile last year.

The 2026 Track World Championships began earlier today with the British team taking part in the men's team pursuit qualifying. The team (Noah Hobbs, Henry Hobbs, Ethan Vernon, and Matthew Bostock) finished second behind Denmark with a time of 3:47.154 and will advance to the first round proper later today.

items.title: Tour of Guangxi: Frits Biesterbos surprises favourites on stage 2 for Picnic PostNL's first WorldTour victory of the season
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
As the WorldTour racing season draws nearer to a close in China, the Dutch team looked set to see out a full season as the only of 18 top-division teams without a win at the highest level. Biesterbos has not only spared their blushes, but with just the team's third victory of any level this season, he's landed them vital UCI points.

Race leader and stage 1 winner Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) finished second at the line in Jingxi, opening up the sprint with the Dutchman waiting to launch from his wheel, with Olav Kooij (Decathlon CMA CGM) charging from a long way back to finish third.

Magnier retains the red jersey heading into the third stage, with Biesterbos six seconds down, and Netcompany Ineos' Sam Welsford staying in third, despite getting boxed out of the final sprint.

Racing on day two in southwest China was focused on the National Road climb (8.5km at 3.4%), which arrived with 35km to go. Two riders from the early breakaway of four survived onto the uphill section: Martin Tjøtta (Uno-X Mobility) and Dries De Bondt (Jayco AlUla), and the attacks started coming from behind.

Jhonatan Narváez (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and Javier Romo (Movistar) bridged across to make it four riders in front, but the new lead group was well controlled by the likes of Soudal-QuickStep and Tudor, trying to keep it together for a sprint.

With that attempt reeled back in 1.5km before the summit, the bunch was calmer, but still active, especially as the race headed towards the intermediate sprint in Huadong. Here, Narváez, Pau Miquel (Bahrain Victorious), and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5) landed the three, two, and one bonus seconds on offer.

A few late attacks were attempted, but they couldn't hold off the now-charging peloton on the flatter run to the line, with Groupama-FDJ United and Decathlon dominating the lead-out into the last 2km. They were overhauled before the finale, though, with Magnier being piloted well into the final corner, but losing out to Biesterbos after hitting the front too early on the drag to the finish.

Racing resumed in China on Thursday on stage 3, with an undulating 212.3km route from Jingxi to Bama, where the likes of Pidcock and Narváez should come to the fore as they look to gain an early advantage in the race for the red jersey.

items.title: Raptors 148, Knicks 98: Scenes from Kawhi’s return
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Having played last night at home, coach Mike Brown rested his starters tonight in Toronto. His opening lineup included Jose Alvarado, Miles McBride, Bruce Brown, Mohamed Diawara, and James Wiseman. Across the aisle, Kawhi Leonard made his preseason debut as the team returned to Scotiabank Arena following a cross-country tour of showcase scrimmages. The Knicks lost to the Timberwolves yesterday, and they dropped another tonight, 148-98. No, Virginia, these games don’t count.

The starters weren’t required to attend, but Mikal Bridges did. Because he’s a savage!

Both teams came out bricking, but the home team fixed their problems sooner, jumping out to a 13-4 lead that chased New York into a timeout. OAKAAKUYOAK RJ Barrett collected an early eight points in seven minutes to lead his team. For our heroes, James Wiseman blanked across the board in the first quarter, with two turnovers that cancelled a pair of rebounds. He played better (offensively, at least) in the second half, finishing the night with 18 points and 10 boards to lead the team.

Midway through the frame, Wiseman sat for Drew Eubanks, who didn’t wow us either, but at least got on the scoreboard. Pacome Dadiet checked in, too, and promptly suffered at the hands of Scottie Barnes—and then Barrett. Not great. (He also played better after intermission.) Seeing Diawara make his first three-pointer of the preseason made us happy, but ‘twas a mere sip while we thirsted for decent basketball. The two Tylers (Kolek, Nickel) checked in with four minutes left in the quarter, and they did little to help. By the break, Barnes had shot 6-of-7 for 15 points, and the score stood at 42-22. The gulf felt much wider than that.

Twice in the first quarter, Mike Brown and Alvarado had extended conversations. They seemed to not be on the same page. To be fair, few Knicks were on the right page tonight.

Toronto opened the second quarter with a 7–0 run, on a bucket from Quickley, a three from Kawhi Leonard, and a drive by Barrett. Tyler Nickel answered with a layup and a three, and Tony Bradley added two baskets inside, but the Knicks played defense like touch football, allowing the Dinos to continue to pour it on. After Bruce Brown’s cutting layup made it 56–33 with 7:16 left, the Raptors went on a 20–2 run. It’s never fun to be on the wrong side of that.

Ja’Kobe Walter scored all eight of his quarter’s points during that stretch, including a three after stripping Wiseman. Jamal Shead dished four dimes on that run, while Leonard added a free throw and a turnaround three. When Collin Murray-Boyles made a putback dunk, Toronto’s advantage reached 76–35.

Leonard had the biggest scoring impact with 11 points in the quarter and 21 in the half. Wiseman gave the Knicks a brief lift late, finishing an Alvarado-assisted dunk and converting a hook shot. Between those baskets, Miles McBride blocked Leonard’s layup (good!) but turned over the rock twice (less good). Alvarado missed two free throws (even less good). Kevin McCullar Jr., Ochai Agbaji and Pacôme Dadiet went scoreless in the period. When the half finally ended, the score was 85–47.

Nickel does have a pretty shot, no?

Through the half, the Knicks’ understudies turned over the ball 12 times compared to Toronto’s two, and were outrebounded 29-17. They’d shot a paltry 22% from deep versus the Raptors’ 40%. McBride and Nickel had eight points apiece for the guests, with no one yet in double digits.

After intermission, the abuse continued with the lead reaching 44 points. New York finally assembled some offense inside: Alvarado hit a pullup, then assisted on buckets by Eubanks and Dadiet. The latter also blocked a Barrett layup, and Eubanks rejected Quickley, but the losses outnumbered the gains. McBride went scoreless during that stretch, missing two threes and having a dunk blocked by Barnes.

Wiseman made the biggest difference for New York after entering at 6:55, scoring nine points on hooks, an alley-oop from Brown, and a putback hook. Jaden Akins (who really does resemble Quinten Grimes from a distance, if you squint) supplied three assists and turned a steal into a layup, while Kolek added a three and two freebies. Together, they powered the Knicks on a 20–9 run that trimmed the score to 109-76. Dadiet contributed seven points, but his fourth foul and Mohamed Diawara’s fifth underscored a general defensive ineptitude. Nickel kept letting shots fly, making just 1-of-9 on the night. After three quarters, the score remained lopsided, 116-70.

In the fourth frame, the differential topped out at 53. New York’s perimeter shooting fell to 17% for the game, a figure that passed the eye test. Your weary blogger fell asleep for a few minutes, but the clang of bricks woke him. Our guys sure left some dents in those Canadian rims. Against Toronto’s third-stringers, Diawara hit another triple (totaled 13 points overall), and Wiseman grabbed five boards. Those were encouraging signs. Less encouraging: Kolek missed four threes down the stretch, McCullar missed two, and Ochai Agbaji and Tony Bradley went scoreless. When it finally was time to go to bed, there was a special satisfaction in turning the TV off on this game.

Back to MSG on Thursday to see the Dinos again. Last game of the preseason, too. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

items.title: Barrios strikes after 53 seconds as Atlético pile misery on 10-man Manchester United
items.author: Sid Lowe at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano
items.content:
Michael Carrick had seen it in his players, he said, but no one else can. Not so far in the Premier League, where they have suffered their worst start in 40 years, and not here in Madrid, where Manchester United’s head coach insisted they would embrace the challenge. The reaction was coming, he promised; he had looked at them and was sure of it. Instead, they were a goal down after just 53 seconds and all that came was the old familiar sting, that early opener from Pablo Barrios and a second from Ademola Lookman condemning them to another defeat.

So much for a reaction, a rebellion: in their place a kind of resignation, a sense that maybe this is just United’s reality: a game that began badly, did not get very much better, and finished even worse. True, the result could have been different, Bryan Mbeumo unable to convert two first-half chances while Bruno Fernandes struck the bar and put an opportunity wide, but that did not diminish the feeling that something is really wrong. It may even have deepened it.

items.title: Gravel Burn introduces 'new dimension' of teams classification at October stage race while schedules revealed for BWR and Grasshopper series - Gravel Bits
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
The second edition of the seven-day Gravel Burn gravel stage race in South Africa, October 25-31, introduces a teams classification with points to determine standings and prizes. It will be the first such classification recognition at a gravel stage race.

Trade teams of three to four riders, as well as alliances of independent riders, will be eligible for the new classification. The top three riders from each team will earn points that will contribute to the daily standings.

Organisers developed the format in collaboration with several individuals, including pro road and gravel veteran Peter Stetina of Canyon x DT Swiss ATR and Adam Hansen, president of the CPA (Cyclistes Professionnels Associés), both having participated in last year’s inaugural race.

"This innovation provides another dimension to the racing and also rewards the riders’ efforts and the teams’ investment," said race founder Kevin Vermaak.

"Independent ‘privateer’ racers formed the foundation of professional gravel racing, adding to the ‘freedom’ and charm of gravel. We recognise that the emergence of ‘superteams’ is a threat to that. That’s why we opened the Teams Classification to all to help level the playing field, where they may form ad-hoc teams to compete with the more formal outfits.”

Canyon x DT Swiss ATR will field a women's team led by former Unbound Gravel 200 winner Carolin Schiff. They will also start two men's teams, one led by former US gravel champion Bradyn Lange. Scott-SRAM will have one team in each division, the women's team including Life Time Grand Prix contender Alexis Skarda and the men's team with Filippo Colombo, who won the UCI Gravel World Series Ceder race in February. Toyota Specialized Imbuko will have two men's teams with all-South African rosters, while Mattia De Marchi will lead a three-rider men's team for The Grip.

The solo race remains the foundation of Nedbank Gravel Burn, with a $150,000 US prize purse split equally between the pro women and pro men categories, including daily payouts to the top 3 and overall top 10. Gravel Burn is a full-service stage race in the Eastern Cape of South Africa, covering 750 kilometres and 8,500 metres of elevation gain.

Among the debutants for individuals are two-time Marathon MTB world champion Henrique Avancini of Brazil, multi-time Japanese XCO mountain bike champion Kohei Yamamoto, as well as 18-year road pro and a former Cape Epic winner Jakob Fuglsang.

Last year's men's champion Matt Beers returns, as well as runner-up Simon Pellaud. Women's champion Axelle Dubau-Prevot will defend her title, lining up against third-placed Hayley Preen.

Five events have been confirmed for the Belgian Waffle Ride schedule next year, with a new Colorado event taking shape. Registration opened October 13 for a quartet of US events spread from March to September, while Mexico takes place in late November.

The sequence of events remains the same, opening in Arizona in early March and then moving to Southern California on May 2, the 16th season for the signature event. The Utah event in Cedar City shifts from June to mid-May, and the Bozeman, Montana event then moves from June to mid-September.

Event organisers Monuments of Gravel are looking to fill the summer with a new event in Colorado, though the location has not been named and it is not known if this will be part of the series. The final ride in the BWR mixed-surface collection will again be held in Mexico on November 21, but is not part of the elite series.

"What began as one questionable idea in San Diego has now carried us through more than 42 events, with a remarkable collection of riders, partners and friends giving it far more life than we could have imagined," noted BWR founder Michael Marckx.

The Quad-Tripel Crown of Gravel series has been offered for several seasons across the US-based collection of events, and will return with the best three of four races determining elite winners. A usual suspect in the series has been Utah, but it may be a standalone race in 2027, according to organisers, and could become a UCI Gravel World Series qualifier.

Belgian Waffle Ride schedule 2027

  • September 18 - BWR Montana

The race schedule for the 2027 Grasshopper Adventure Series, now in its 30th year, was released with five races in northern California. The opener takes place at Low Gap on January 31, a 59-mile gravel event with 95% dirt tracks in Ukiah, and culminates at Ukiah Mendo Epic on May 23, a 70-mile mixed-terrain adventure in the same area.

The middle of the schedule includes the classic mixed-terrain Huffmaster on February 28, the road and climbing-heavy King Ridge on March 20 and the gravel-singletrack challenge of Jackson Forest on April 10.

Registration is open, and a series pass for all five events is $675, plus fees, with individual races at $155 each. Prices go up after November 30, two months before the opener.

Last year, Jen Tavé (SpeedBlock-Terún Pro Cycling) and Cassius Anderson (Marin Service Course) secured the overall titles for elite divisions in the five-race Grasshopper Series.

Grasshopper Adventure Series schedule 2027

  • January 31 - Low Gap at Ukiah, California
  • February 28 - Huffmaster at Maxwell, California
  • March 20 - King Ridge at Guerneville, California
  • April 10 - Jackson Forest at Casper, California
  • May 23 - Ukiah Mendo Epic at Ukiah, California

items.title: Eneco Tour: Jakob Söderqvist secures leader's jersey as fastest rider in nighttime prologue at The Hague
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) won the prologue Tuesday night in The Hague to take the first leader's jersey of the Eneco Tour.

Sweden's time trial champion was the third-to-last rider on the 3.1km course and posted a winning time of 3 minutes, 32 seconds. A surprising time just seven-tenths of a second slower gave 23-year old Wessel Mouris (Unibet Rose Rockets) second place. Last year's stage race GC winner Christophe Laporte (Visma-Lease a Bike) was third, 1.4 seconds behind the winner.

"These prologues are so much adrenaline, and you're really in a hot box in the end and super on your nerves when you cross the finish line," Söderqvist said to TV cameras at the finish.

He had no idea how tight the times were, and said "oh, better buy a lottery ticket then" when told his time was half a second better than Wessel Mouris.

"I had a pleasure to have a couple of days in orange also last year, and to be back here with good enough shape to start it even better."

For a while it looked like both Mouris brothers would grab podium spots, with Michiel Mouris (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) going second to his brother. Then the final four riders in the final wave shook the standings on scorching rides.

Great Britain's time trial champion Ethan Hayter (Soudal-QuickStep), who won the prologue last year, knocked Michiel Mouris down a spot with a faster time by 1 second. Then Laporte and Söderqvist dispatched the 19-year-old to fifth place, Hayter going fourth, and one brother on the podium.

The recreated Tour of Holland, now Eneco Tour, made a return last year after a 21-year absence from the UCI calendar, and the composition of two time trials and four road stages was replicated for the 2026 edition. However, the twist this year was that all six days of racing integrated racing for pro women, formerly the Ladies Tour of Holland. The blend of staggered start times and similar routes using circuits began with the Prologue.

The action began Tuesday with a unique process for the 3.1km prologue - waves of women and men sharing the same course. The first 28 women took the start in The Hague at one-minute intervals followed by a five-minute break and then the first 28 men hit the course with the same spacing. This pattern for alternating waves was repeated, with a total of 88 women and 88 men on the start list, the early riders seeing the sun setting while the city course became illuminated by street lamps in the darkness.

The start ramp was inside the Sportcampus Zuiderpark multi-functional arena, Robbe Claeys (Volkerwessels Cycling) the first men's rider down the ramp at 18:34 local time for a quick lap around the park, and setting the standard at 3:52.

Nils Eekhoff (Picnic PostNL) took over the hot seat just six riders later with 3:47, and then was dispatched by Joeri Schaper (Soudal-QuickStep) who went four seconds faster.

The second wave of 30 riders started with Thor Verleysen (Volkerwessels Cycling). Eight riders later, Hartthijs De Vries (Unibet Rose Rockets) flew across the course as the first rider to go under three minutes, 40 seconds, posting 3:39. He was nearly knocked off the hot seat by Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike), who came through six-tenths of a second slower.

It was De Vries' teammate Thomáš Kopecký who then took over with 3:37. He held the best time as only Pepijn Reinderink (Soudal-QuickStep) came within one second from the next six riders completing the middle wave.

The final wave saw 23-year-old Wessel Mouris grab the lead in a time of 3:33. The TV camera showed him smiling broadly when his brother, Michiel Mouris almost took the spotlight, going just two seconds slower. The brothers, however, were one-two with 15 riders to go.

The last three riders featured Söderqvist, Laporte and New Zealand TT champion Finn Fischer-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe). Söderqvist stormed around the circuit for the best time, with Laporte getting a podium spot, but Fisher-Black coming up short in sixth.

After the prologue, stage 1 takes place in Ede with a flat 40-kilometre circuit that the men tackle three times and women twice. The men's stage begins after the women's finish.
