items.title: Eneco Tour Women: Lieke Nooijen dominates prologue for first race leader's jersey
items.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
items.content:
Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) secured the prologue victory and took the first leader's jersey at the Eneco Tour Women. The Dutch rider covered the 3.1km course with the fastest time of 3:51, beating her compatriots Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) and Lonneke Uneken (VolkerWessels) by eight seconds in The Hague.

Nooijen started her time trial in the third of three waves, surpassing both Kool, who posted the early benchmark and had sat in the hot seat since the opening wave, and Uneken to take the day's spoils.

The Dutch road race national champion now leads the overall classification heading into stage 1 in Ede on Wednesday.

"I'm super happy with this victory. I've worked really hard towards this, so it's great to win such a short prologue by eight seconds," she said.

"I went full gas from the start and managed to maintain my speed throughout. These short efforts really suit me, and that paid off today."

This year all six days of racing will integrate stages for pro women, formerly the Ladies Tour of Holland, and for pro men, formerly the NIBC Tour of Holland, with staggered start times and similar routes.

The action began Tuesday with a unique process for the 3.1km prologue - waves of women and men sharing the same course. The first 30 women took the start in The Hague at one-minute intervals, followed by a five-minute break, and then the first 30 men hit the course with the same spacing. This alternating-wave pattern repeated, with a total of 88 women and 88 men on the start list.

During the first wave of the women's prologue, Kool posted the fastest time of 3:59, averaging nearly 17kph across the 3.1km course. Femke Markus (SD Worx-Protime) and Margaux Vigié (Visma-Lease a Bike) were both three seconds slower in second and third place

However, the second wave started about thirty minutes with three riders slotting in behind Kool; Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché Ladies) stormed into the runner's-up spot just a fraction of a second slower, Maud Rijnbeek (VolkerWessels) a two seconds back and Letizia Borghesi (AG Insurance-Soudal) at three seconds back, bumping Markus and Vigié out of the top three.

The third wave on course would decide the final top placings of the prologue, and while Kool was the day's leader for much of this event, her time was encroached upon by Uneken, who stormed across the finish line with the second-fastest time of the day, a fraction of a second slower than Kool.

But there would be one faster rider on course to surpass them both, with Nooijen putting a stamp on the prologue with the victory and the event's first leader's jersey.

items.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Manchester City unrepentant in victory, Spurs make progress of a sort and Noni Madueke meets the moment

The manner of Manchester City’s victory at Liverpool was an article of both vindication and vilification. Those gleefully wielding inflatable bananas in the Anfield away end could thumb their noses. Why not enjoy the dances of defiance until the music stops? The same went for City players, asked to perform under the darkest of clouds, able to focus, at last, on football, rather than legal argument and uncertain futures. Beyond City, the sight of a club found guilty of 100-plus charges laying waste to such rivals as Liverpool was deeply uncomfortable. The Premier League season and product are badly damaged until the matter is somehow resolved. What happened at Anfield should double the haste for a resolution. Chants of “cheat” whenever City players, the game already won, slipped the ball around, are bound to be repeated at other stadiums. Enzo Maresca has described his club’s plight as “noise” but his team’s victory did absolutely nothing to turn the volume down.

items.title: Manchester United and Spurs come back to reality as City saga offers brief distraction | John Brewin
items.author: John Brewin at Old Trafford
items.content:
Manchester City’s rule breaches have dominated headlines and shifted focus from both clubs’ self-inflicted wounds

Turning back the clock is impossible. Up in the Stretford End’s middle tier, the ticker had returned, a retouching job to “51 years” invoiced for the pertinent sum of £114. The Manchester City that existed before the Abu Dhabi project won their last trophy in 1976. Questionable maths is perhaps not confined to the Etihad’s accounts department, though Manchester United’s support must get their kicks where they can.

Should City’s fall from grace be fully confirmed by the appeals and sanctions process, there is nothing in the way of irrefutable evidence of United’s former supremacy being restored. How United fans would love to return to 2008, when Michael Carrick was a key cog in Sir Alex Ferguson’s team of European champions. Instead, the autumn of 2026 brings a familiar swell of doubt, another manager dragged towards the meat grinder. It will be 40 years next month since Ferguson was appointed. A draw made United’s start to their league campaign the worst since then. The Carrick bounce has come to a standstill.
